title: Near-Optimal Second-Order Convex Finite-Sum Optimization under Individual Smoothness
abstract: arXiv:2610.42040v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study the stochastic second-order oracle complexity of solving smooth convex finite-sum optimization with $n$ components. Very recently, Tsedenov \& Kovalev (2026) showed that the minimax optimal complexity under averaged smoothness and convexity is $\tilde{\Theta}(n + n^{6/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$ by establishing nearly matching upper and lower bounds. In this paper, we show that individual smoothness and convexity provably enable further acceleration, where the lower complexity bound is $\Omega(n+ n^{5/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$ under this stronger assumption. Then, by establishing a novel second-order self-bounding inequality, we design a new Taylor-corrected lazy Newton method, which can lead to a better complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n + n^{5/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$ by applying the optimal Monteiro-Svaiter acceleration, matching our lower bound up to only logarithmic factors.

translated_title: 个体光滑性条件下近最优的二阶凸有限和优化
translated_abstract: 我们研究了求解具有 n 个分量的光滑凸有限和优化问题的随机二阶预言机复杂度。最近，Tsedenov 与 Kovalev（2026）通过建立几乎匹配的上界与下界，证明了在平均光滑性和凸性条件下的极小极大最优复杂度为 $\tilde{\Theta}(n + n^{6/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$。在本文中，我们证明了个体光滑性和凸性能够带来可证明的进一步加速，在这一更强假设下，复杂度下界为 $\Omega(n + n^{5/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$。随后，通过建立一种新颖的二阶自界定不等式，我们设计了一种新的泰勒修正惰性牛顿方法，通过应用最优的 Monteiro-Svaiter 加速技术，可以达到更好的复杂度 $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n + n^{5/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$，该结果与我们的下界仅相差对数因子。
tldr: 本文证明了个体光滑性与凸性假设可将二阶凸有限和优化的复杂度下界改进为 $\Omega(n + n^{5/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$，并通过提出新颖的二阶自界定不等式和泰勒修正惰性牛顿方法，结合最优 Monteiro-Svaiter 加速，实现了与下界仅差对数因子的近最优算法复杂度。
en_tdlr: This paper proves that individual smoothness and convexity improve the lower bound for second-order convex finite-sum optimization to $\Omega(n + n^{5/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$, and achieves a matching near-optimal complexity, up to logarithmic factors, via a novel second-order self-bounding inequality and a Taylor-corrected lazy Newton method combined with optimal Monteiro-Svaiter acceleration.
